headline: Gemini's cheaper AI tier hits severe rate limits, frustrating users with frequent blocks
summary: A user found Gemini's cheaper Google AI Plus plan (AUD 15/month) so heavily rate-limited that it became "barely worth keeping," despite initially preferring it over Claude.
details: Six months ago, a user nearly canceled Claude, finding Gemini 3 Pro superior for coding and general exploration. Gemini's premium tier, costing around AUD 30/month, offered robust image and video generation, making it the preferred AI tool.

However, Claude significantly improved over time in areas like coding accuracy, front-end output, and agent behavior. The user noticed week-to-week improvements, leading them to trust Claude's responses more often for critical tasks.

As Claude became the primary tool for serious work, the user downgraded Gemini to the Google AI Plus tier, priced at AUD 15/month. This cheaper plan was intended for lighter use, like quick searches or minor queries.

Even at this low-stakes level, the Google AI Plus tier frequently imposes rate limits, often returning messages like "I'm having a hard time fulfilling your request." The user reported losing access to the better model completely and hitting flat rate limits.

The user concludes that the issue isn't Gemini's capability but the restrictive nature of the cheaper plan. Paying less doesn't just mean a less powerful model; it means less tolerance for usage, signaling that lower-paying users are not a priority.

headline_marked: [[Google Play Store opens to third-party billing]] globally, new fee structure begins June 2026
headline: Google Play Store opens to third-party billing globally, new fee structure begins June 2026
summary: Google will allow developers to offer alternative billing options and is restructuring its service fees, with a global rollout starting in June 2026 for some regions and extending to 2027 worldwide.
details: Google announced major policy changes for the Play Store in March, and has now set the dates for these changes to go live. The primary shift involves opening the Play Store billing system to third-party options, moving away from Google's exclusive system.

This new policy allows developers to offer alternative billing methods directly within their apps or guide users to their own websites for purchases. Developers will also have the freedom to design their own choice screens, provided they adhere to Google's UX guidelines.

The 'Billing Choice' program will first become available on June 30, 2026, for developers selling apps and services in the EEA, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It will then expand to Australia on September 30, 2026, followed by Japan and South Korea on December 31, 2026. The rest of the world is scheduled for a rollout on September 30, 2027.

Alongside opening billing options, Google is restructuring its developer fees into two categories: a service fee and a billing fee. This new fee structure will also take effect on June 30, 2026, in the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Economic Area.

Google will charge a 10% service fee on the first $1 million of annual revenue, applicable regardless of whether Google Play billing is used. Once annual revenue surpasses $1 million, this fee increases to 20% for new installs and 25% for existing installs.

Developers who choose to continue using Google Play billing will incur an additional 5% billing fee. This extra 5% charge will not apply to transactions processed through third-party payment options, though those options will have their own processing charges.

Apps that qualify for the 'Games Level Up' and 'Apps Experience' programs will benefit from a reduced 15% service fee on transactions after their annual revenue exceeds $1 million. These specific programs are set to go live later in 2026, starting in September, and require developers to meet certain criteria.
